title: The First Principle of Teaching
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: Stuart borrows the idea of first-principles reasoning, illustrated by the Declaration of Independence, to ask what the first principle of education is. He notes that the founders applied their principles imperfectly, but argues that first principles still let people see opportunity where others see an impasse and think clearly amid complexity. His answer is that schools exist to promote the long-term flourishing of students. He presents this as the core of the work, beneath philosophical debates, stylistic differences, policy wars and standards. Against the constant flow of initiatives, fads, research and tasks, he offers long-term flourishing as a charm against overwhelm.

quotes: When you approach a problem by first stripping it down to its most elemental parts, that's a “first principles” approach to problem-solving.

Here's the point: First principles make it possible for us to see opportunities where others see an impasse. They let us think clearly in the face of interminable complexity.
Schools exist to promote the long-term flourishing of students. This is the core of our work, beneath the philosophical debates and stylistic differences and policy wars and standards and so on.
In light of the perpetual onslaught of initiatives and fads and research and “research” and tasks and minutiae we face daily, we must be clear on the first principle of education.
Long-term flourishing (or LTF, as my colleagues and I sometimes refer to it) — that's what we do. May it be emblazoned on our hearts as a charm against the overwhelm.
